title: Reactions, Kinetics and Equilibrium
bigQuestion: What decides whether a reaction happens, how fast it goes, how far it goes, and whether we can push it further?

story.title: Bread from the Air
story.kicker: The air is four fifths nitrogen, yet crops were starving for it, until a chemist found a way to force the stubborn gas into fertilizer.
paragraphs: In 1898 the British chemist William Crookes gave a speech that alarmed his audience. Wheat, he said, was running out of nitrogen. Plants need nitrogen to build proteins, and farmers had been feeding fields with guano from Peruvian islands and sodium nitrate mined in the Chilean desert. Both were being dug out faster than nature replaced them. Yet every acre of farmland sat under thousands of tons of nitrogen gas. The problem was that the two nitrogen atoms in N2 are joined by a triple bond so strong that almost nothing pulls them apart.

Fritz Haber, a chemist in Karlsruhe, Germany, attacked the problem with equilibrium theory. Nitrogen and hydrogen can combine to form ammonia, NH3, but the reaction is reversible and at ordinary conditions only a trace forms. Haber worked out that high pressure would push the reaction toward ammonia, that a catalyst could speed it up, and that the temperature had to be a careful compromise: hot enough to go fast, cool enough to favor the product. In July 1909 his tabletop apparatus produced a steady drip of liquid ammonia.

Turning a drip into an industry took Carl Bosch and the chemical company BASF. Bosch's engineers had to build steel vessels that could hold hydrogen at pressures of hundreds of atmospheres without cracking, and test thousands of catalyst recipes until a cheap iron-based one worked. The first full plant opened at Oppau in 1913. Ammonia could be turned into nitrate fertilizer, and the world's food supply was no longer chained to Chilean mines.

The same ammonia could also be turned into explosives, and Germany used it that way in the First World War. Haber himself directed the first large chlorine gas attack in 1915, a fact that has shadowed his name ever since. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the ammonia synthesis, and Bosch shared one in 1931 for high-pressure methods. Science and its uses do not always point the same direction.

Today the Haber-Bosch process makes well over a hundred million tons of ammonia a year. Many scientists estimate that the nitrogen in the food of roughly half the world's people passed through it. Drive through Illinois farmland in spring and you will see white tanks of anhydrous ammonia being pulled across the fields. Every one of them is a monument to a chemist who learned to bargain with an equilibrium.
story.think: Haber's reaction needed high pressure, a catalyst and a compromise temperature. Why do you think each of those three choices was necessary?

lessons.title: Sorting Reactions
lessons.mainIdea: Chemical reactions rearrange atoms without creating or destroying them, and most fall into a few recognizable patterns.
reading: Strike a match and wood becomes ash, smoke and heat. Leave a bicycle in the rain and shiny steel turns to orange rust. In every *chemical reaction*, bonds break and new bonds form, but the atoms themselves survive. Antoine Lavoisier established this in the 1780s by weighing everything that went into a sealed reaction and everything that came out. The totals matched. This is the law of *conservation of mass*, and it is why a chemical equation must be balanced, with the same count of each atom on both sides.

Chemists group reactions by their shape. In a *synthesis* reaction, two or more substances join to make one, as when hydrogen and oxygen form water. In *decomposition*, one substance splits into simpler ones, as when hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen. In a single replacement, one element takes the place of another in a compound. In a double replacement, two compounds swap partners, often dropping an insoluble solid, called a precipitate, out of solution.

*Combustion* is a reaction with oxygen that releases heat and light. Burning methane gives carbon dioxide and water: CH4 + 2 O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O. Count the atoms. One carbon, four hydrogens and four oxygens on each side. The coefficient 2 in front of O2 is not decoration. It tells you that one methane molecule needs two oxygen molecules. Balanced equations let chemists predict how much product a given amount of fuel, ore or medicine will yield before anything is mixed.

words.d: a change in which bonds break and form so that starting substances turn into different substances
the law that atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction, so total mass stays the same
a reaction in which two or more substances combine to form one product
a reaction in which one substance breaks apart into two or more simpler substances
a reaction with oxygen that gives off heat and usually light, such as burning

look.title: Lavoisier Weighs the Evidence
look.text: Lavoisier wrote that nothing is created in the operations of art or of nature, and that it may be stated as a principle that in every operation there is an equal quantity of matter before and after. The quality and quantity of the elements remain the same, he wrote; only changes and modifications occur. On this principle, he said, the whole art of performing chemical experiments depends.
look.cite: Antoine Lavoisier, Elementary Treatise on Chemistry, 1789
look.prompt: Lavoisier could not see atoms. What kind of measurement let him state this principle with such confidence?

check.q: Why must a chemical equation be balanced?
choices: Because atoms are conserved: the same number of each must appear on both sides
Because reactions always produce equal volumes
Because the products must weigh less than the reactants
Because every reaction makes exactly two products
check.why: Lavoisier's law of conservation of mass means atoms are only rearranged, never created or lost.

check.q: Hydrogen peroxide, H2O2, breaks down into water and oxygen gas. What type of reaction is this?
check.why: One compound splits into simpler substances, the definition of decomposition.

check.q: In the equation CH4 + 2 O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O, what does the 2 in front of O2 mean?
choices: Oxygen has two atoms in its nucleus
Two oxygen molecules are needed for each methane molecule
Oxygen is twice as heavy as methane
check.why: Coefficients give the ratio of molecules, which balances the count of oxygen atoms on each side.

lessons.title: Electrons on the Move: Redox
lessons.mainIdea: In a redox reaction one substance loses electrons and another gains them, and this transfer powers rusting, burning and batteries.
reading: Many reactions are really about electrons changing hands. When iron rusts, each iron atom gives up electrons and becomes an iron ion, while oxygen takes those electrons. Losing electrons is *oxidation*. Gaining electrons is *reduction*. The two always happen together, because an electron lost must go somewhere. Chemists call the pair a *redox* reaction. A handy memory aid is OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain.

To track electrons, chemists assign each atom an *oxidation number*, a bookkeeping charge. A free element is 0. In compounds, oxygen is usually −2 and hydrogen +1, and the numbers in a neutral compound add to zero. When iron metal (0) becomes iron in rust (+3), its oxidation number rose, so it was oxidized. Oxygen went from 0 to −2, so it was reduced. The substance that takes electrons, here oxygen, is the oxidizing agent. The one that gives them, iron, is the reducing agent.

Redox runs the world. Burning any fuel oxidizes carbon and hydrogen. Your cells oxidize glucose slowly and capture the released energy. Photosynthesis runs the same chemistry in reverse, reducing carbon dioxide into sugar using sunlight. A battery is a redox reaction with the electrons forced to travel through a wire on their way from one substance to the other. Bleach whitens by oxidizing colored molecules. Understanding who gives and who takes electrons is the first step in every one of these.

words.d: the loss of electrons by an atom, ion or molecule during a reaction
the gain of electrons by an atom, ion or molecule during a reaction
a reaction in which electrons move from one substance to another; oxidation and reduction together
a bookkeeping charge assigned to an atom to track whether it has gained or lost electrons

look.title: The Nail and the Copper Solution
look.text: Drop a clean iron nail into a blue solution of copper sulfate. Within minutes the nail grows a fuzzy brown-red coat of copper metal, and over an hour the blue of the solution fades toward pale green. Iron atoms are leaving the nail as ions, and copper ions from the solution are becoming solid copper on its surface.
look.prompt: Which substance is oxidized and which is reduced? Explain what the fading blue color tells you about where the electrons went.

check.q: What happens to an atom that is oxidized?
check.why: Oxidation is the loss of electrons; OIL RIG.

check.q: Why can oxidation never happen alone?
choices: The electrons lost by one substance must be gained by another
Every atom already has a full shell
check.why: Electrons are conserved. A loss by one species is a gain by another, so reduction always accompanies oxidation.

check.q: In the rusting of iron, which substance is the oxidizing agent?
choices: Oxygen, because it takes the electrons
Water, because it dissolves the rust
check.why: The oxidizing agent is the one that accepts electrons and is itself reduced. Oxygen does that.

lessons.title: Energy In, Energy Out
lessons.mainIdea: Breaking bonds costs energy and forming bonds releases it, so the difference decides whether a reaction gives off heat or absorbs it.
reading: A hand warmer grows hot; a cold pack grows icy. Both are chemical reactions, and the difference lies in bonds. Breaking a bond always costs energy, because the atoms are being pulled apart against their attraction. Forming a bond always releases energy. If the new bonds are stronger than the old ones, the reaction gives off heat overall and is *exothermic*. If the new bonds are weaker, the reaction must take heat from its surroundings and is *endothermic*.

The energy of a chemical system is called its *enthalpy*, and the change in enthalpy during a reaction is written as ΔH. A negative ΔH means energy left the system as heat: exothermic. A positive ΔH means energy entered: endothermic. Burning methane has a ΔH of about −890 kJ per mole, a large release, which is why natural gas heats homes across Illinois. Dissolving ammonium nitrate in water is endothermic, and that is what makes a cold pack cold.

You can estimate ΔH from *bond energies*, the average energy needed to break a particular bond. Add up the energy to break every bond in the reactants, subtract the energy released by forming every bond in the products, and the result is roughly ΔH. Hydrogen and chlorine, for example, break an H-H bond and a Cl-Cl bond and form two much stronger H-Cl bonds, so the reaction is strongly exothermic. This is the accounting behind every fuel: the products, usually carbon dioxide and water, have exceptionally strong bonds.

words.d: describes a reaction that releases heat to its surroundings
describes a reaction that absorbs heat from its surroundings
the heat content of a system; its change, ΔH, is the heat released or absorbed in a reaction at constant pressure
the average energy needed to break one mole of a particular kind of bond

look.title: Average Bond Energies
look.prompt: Use the table to estimate the energy change when H2 and Cl2 form 2 HCl. Is the reaction exothermic or endothermic, and which numbers told you?

check.q: Which statement about bonds and energy is always true?
choices: Breaking bonds costs energy and forming bonds releases it
Bonds have no effect on the energy of a reaction
check.why: Atoms attract each other in a bond, so pulling them apart takes energy and letting them join gives it back.

check.q: A reaction has a ΔH of +50 kJ/mol. What will you observe?
choices: The container gets cold as heat is absorbed
check.why: A positive ΔH means the system takes in heat from its surroundings, which is endothermic.

check.q: Why is the reaction of hydrogen with chlorine exothermic?
choices: The two H-Cl bonds formed are stronger overall than the H-H and Cl-Cl bonds broken
check.why: More energy is released by forming the two strong H-Cl bonds than is spent breaking the reactant bonds.

lessons.title: Collisions That Count
lessons.mainIdea: Reactions happen when particles collide with enough energy and the right orientation, so anything that increases effective collisions speeds the reaction up.
reading: Iron rusts over years; a match head burns in a second. Both are reactions with oxygen. The *reaction rate*, how fast reactants turn into products, varies enormously. *Collision theory* explains why. For molecules to react they must first collide. But most collisions are useless. The molecules must hit hard enough to start breaking bonds and must be lined up so the right atoms touch. Only these effective collisions count.

Anything that raises the number of effective collisions raises the rate. Higher *concentration* packs more molecules into the same space, so collisions happen more often. Higher temperature makes molecules move faster, so they collide more often and, more importantly, hit harder. Near room temperature, a rise of about 10 °C often doubles the rate of a reaction, which is why food spoils quickly on a summer counter and slowly in the refrigerator.

For solids, only the surface can react. Grinding a solid into powder multiplies its *surface area*, and the rate climbs. A log burns slowly; sawdust of the same wood can explode. Grain elevators across Illinois have been destroyed by dust explosions for exactly this reason: fine grain dust suspended in air presents so much surface that a spark sets off the whole cloud at once. Mills fight it with ventilation and by keeping dust from building up.

words.d: how quickly reactants are used up or products form, often in moles per liter per second
the idea that particles react only when they collide with enough energy and the right orientation
the amount of a substance in a given volume of solution or gas
the total exposed area of a solid; more surface area means more places for reaction

look.title: Two Tablets, Two Glasses
look.text: Drop a whole antacid tablet into a glass of cold water and a crushed tablet into a second glass of the same cold water. Start a timer. The crushed one fizzes furiously and disappears well before the whole one is half gone. Now repeat with two whole tablets, one in cold water and one in warm.
look.prompt: Predict which tablet finishes first in each pair, and explain both results using collision theory.

check.q: According to collision theory, why do most collisions between reactant molecules not produce a reaction?
choices: They lack enough energy or the right orientation
Reactions only happen at the surface of a liquid
The products form and immediately break apart
check.why: Only collisions with enough energy and the right alignment can break the necessary bonds.

check.q: Why does a refrigerator slow the spoiling of food?
choices: Lower temperature means slower, weaker collisions between molecules
check.why: Reaction rate drops steeply as temperature falls because fewer collisions carry enough energy.

check.q: Why can grain dust explode while a pile of grain only burns slowly?
choices: Dust is a different chemical from grain
A pile of grain is too cold to burn
Dust has enormous surface area, so nearly all of it can react at once
check.why: Surface area controls how much solid is exposed to oxygen. A cloud of fine dust is almost all surface.

lessons.title: The Hill Every Reaction Must Climb
lessons.mainIdea: Reactions need a minimum energy, the activation energy, and a catalyst speeds a reaction by offering a lower path over that hill.
reading: Gasoline sits in a tank for months without burning, even though burning would release a huge amount of energy. Why? Before the strong new bonds can form, the old bonds must start to break, and that costs energy up front. The minimum energy colliding molecules need to react is the *activation energy*. Think of a hill between the reactants' valley and the products' valley. A spark gives a few molecules enough energy to cross, and the heat they release pushes the rest over.

In 1889 Svante Arrhenius showed that reaction rate depends on the fraction of molecules with energy above this hill, and that this fraction rises steeply with temperature. That is the real reason heating speeds reactions so much. It is not just that molecules collide more often; a far larger share of them collide hard enough. A reaction with a high activation energy can be almost frozen at room temperature and fast at a few hundred degrees.

A *catalyst* is a substance that speeds a reaction without being used up. It works by offering a different route with a lower hill. The iron in the Haber process, the platinum and rhodium in a car's catalytic converter that turn exhaust gases into less harmful ones, and the *enzymes* in your cells are all catalysts. An enzyme can make a reaction go millions of times faster at body temperature. Without catalysts, digestion would take years and the chemical industry would grind to a halt.

words.d: the minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur
a substance that speeds up a reaction by providing a lower-energy path, and is not used up
a protein that acts as a catalyst in living things

look.title: Arrhenius Explains the Effect of Heat
look.text: Arrhenius proposed that in any reacting mixture only a small fraction of the molecules are in an active, high-energy form, and that only these can react. He showed that the number of such active molecules grows very rapidly with temperature, much faster than the speed of the molecules does, and that this explains why a modest rise in temperature so greatly increases the rate of a reaction.
look.cite: Svante Arrhenius, paper on the rate of inversion of cane sugar by acids, 1889
look.prompt: Arrhenius said only 'active' molecules react. How does this idea connect to the picture of a hill that reactants must climb?

check.q: Why does gasoline not burn on its own in a tank, even though burning releases energy?
choices: Its molecules must first get over an activation energy barrier
Gasoline is not flammable at room temperature
There is no oxygen in a tank
check.why: Bonds must begin to break before new ones form, and that initial cost is the activation energy.

check.q: How does a catalyst speed a reaction?
choices: It raises the temperature of the mixture
It provides a path with a lower activation energy
It makes the products more stable
check.why: A catalyst offers a different, lower hill, so more collisions have enough energy to react.

check.q: A catalytic converter uses platinum to speed the reaction of exhaust gases. After years of driving, what has happened to the platinum?
choices: It has been converted into carbon dioxide
It is still there, because a catalyst is not used up
It has all been used up
check.why: Catalysts take part in the reaction but are regenerated, so the same platinum works over and over.

lessons.title: Step by Step: Mechanisms
lessons.mainIdea: Most reactions happen in a series of elementary steps, and the slowest step sets the overall rate.
reading: A balanced equation shows the start and the end, not the route. Most reactions do not happen in one collision. They proceed through a *reaction mechanism*, a sequence of *elementary steps*, each of them a single collision or a single bond breaking. Between steps, short-lived *intermediates* form and are used up. Chemists piece together mechanisms by measuring how the rate changes when they change each concentration.

In a multistep mechanism, one step is usually much slower than the others. That *rate-determining step* controls the overall rate, just as the slowest cashier controls how fast a line moves no matter how quick the others are. A *rate law* is an equation that links the rate to the concentrations of the substances involved in that slow step. If doubling the concentration of a reactant doubles the rate, the rate is first order in that reactant. If it quadruples, second order.

Mechanisms explained one of the great environmental problems of the late twentieth century. In 1974 Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland showed that chlorine atoms released from CFC refrigerants high in the atmosphere destroy ozone in a two-step cycle. A chlorine atom takes an oxygen from ozone, then gives it up again and is regenerated. Because the chlorine is not consumed, one atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules. That catalytic mechanism led to the 1987 Montreal Protocol, a treaty phasing out CFCs, and the ozone layer has slowly begun to recover.

words.d: the sequence of individual steps by which a reaction actually occurs
a single collision or bond change that happens exactly as written, one event at a time
a substance formed in one step of a mechanism and used up in a later step
the slowest step of a mechanism, which sets the overall rate of the reaction
an equation that relates the rate of a reaction to the concentrations of the reactants

look.title: The Slow Cashier
look.text: A store has three steps at checkout: a scanner that takes 5 seconds per customer, a cashier who takes 60 seconds, and a bagger who takes 10 seconds. The manager buys a faster scanner that takes 1 second. The line moves no faster. Then the manager adds a second cashier, and the line speeds up almost twofold.
look.prompt: Which step is rate-determining? What would this suggest about where a chemist should look to speed up a multistep reaction?

check.q: What is an intermediate in a reaction mechanism?
choices: A catalyst that is added at the start
A substance made in one step and consumed in a later step
check.why: Intermediates appear during the mechanism but not in the overall balanced equation.

check.q: A reaction has a fast first step and a slow second step. What controls the overall rate?
check.why: The slowest step is the bottleneck, so it determines the rate.

check.q: Why can a single chlorine atom destroy thousands of ozone molecules?
choices: Chlorine is much heavier than ozone
The chlorine atom is regenerated after each cycle, acting as a catalyst
Ozone is unstable and would break down anyway
Chlorine reacts with all three oxygen atoms at once
check.why: The mechanism returns the chlorine atom unchanged, so it is free to attack another ozone molecule.

lessons.title: Reactions That Run Both Ways
lessons.mainIdea: In a closed system, a reversible reaction reaches a dynamic equilibrium where forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations stop changing.
reading: Seal nitrogen dioxide, a brown gas, in a flask. The color fades partway as molecules pair up into colorless dinitrogen tetroxide, and then it stops fading. It never becomes fully colorless. Both gases are present, and their amounts hold steady. This is *equilibrium*. But the molecules have not stopped. The forward reaction continues, and so does the reverse. They just run at the same rate, so nothing changes overall. The state is *dynamic*, like a crowd where people enter and leave a room at exactly equal rates.

Every *reversible reaction* in a closed container heads toward equilibrium. Where it settles depends on the reaction. Some sit far toward products, some far toward reactants. Chemists describe the position with the *equilibrium constant*, K, the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations at equilibrium, each raised to the power of its coefficient. A large K means mostly products. A tiny K means the reaction barely goes. K depends on temperature and nothing else.

Equilibrium is everywhere you look. Carbon dioxide dissolved in a soda is in equilibrium with the gas above it, until you open the cap and let the gas escape. Oxygen binds to hemoglobin in your lungs, where it is plentiful, and unbinds in your muscles, where it is scarce. Stalactites grow as dissolved calcium carbonate slowly comes out of equilibrium with cave water. Understanding equilibrium means understanding why reactions stop where they do, and what it would take to move them.

words.d: the state of a reversible reaction in which forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant
constantly in motion; at equilibrium both reactions keep running even though nothing seems to change
a reaction whose products can react to re-form the reactants
K, the ratio of product to reactant concentrations at equilibrium; large K means the reaction favors products

look.title: The Escalator Runner
look.text: A runner jogs up a down escalator. When she runs faster than the stairs move, she rises. When she tires, she sinks. At one particular speed she stays exactly level, feet moving, stairs moving, position unchanged. From across the mall she appears to be standing still.
look.prompt: How is the runner like a reaction at equilibrium? What in the picture stands for the forward and reverse reactions, and what stands for the concentrations?

check.q: At equilibrium, what is true about the forward and reverse reactions?
check.why: Equilibrium is dynamic. Both keep running, but at matched rates, so concentrations hold steady.

check.q: A reaction has a very large equilibrium constant. What does that tell you?
choices: At equilibrium, mostly products are present
check.why: K compares products to reactants. A large K means products dominate. K says nothing about speed.

check.q: Why does opening a soda bottle change the equilibrium between dissolved and gaseous carbon dioxide?
choices: The system is no longer closed, so gas escapes and dissolved CO2 keeps leaving to replace it
The temperature of the soda rises
check.why: Equilibrium requires a closed system. Once gas escapes, the reverse process cannot keep up.

lessons.title: Pushing an Equilibrium
lessons.mainIdea: When an equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts in the direction that partly undoes the change, a rule known as Le Châtelier's principle.
reading: In 1884 the French chemist Henry Le Châtelier stated a rule that lets chemists steer reactions. If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the disturbance. This is *Le Châtelier's principle*. Add more reactant, and the system uses some of it up by making more product. Remove a product as it forms, and the reaction keeps making more to replace it. Industry uses that second trick constantly.

Pressure matters for gases. Squeeze a gas mixture and the equilibrium shifts toward whichever side has fewer molecules, because fewer molecules take up less room and relieve some of the pressure. In the ammonia reaction, four molecules of gas, one N2 and three H2, become two molecules of NH3. High pressure therefore pushes hard toward ammonia. That is why Haber and Bosch needed vessels rated for hundreds of atmospheres.

Temperature is the subtle one. Heat behaves like a product in an exothermic reaction. Raising the temperature is like adding product, so the equilibrium shifts back toward reactants. Lowering it shifts toward products. Ammonia formation is exothermic, so cooling favors ammonia. But temperature is also the only disturbance that changes K itself, and cold reactions are slow. A chemist who wants both a good yield and a fast rate is caught between kinetics and equilibrium. The next lesson shows how Haber cut that deal.

words.d: the rule that a disturbed equilibrium shifts in the direction that partly cancels the disturbance
a change in the amounts of reactants and products as an equilibrium moves to a new balance
the force gas molecules exert on their container; raising it favors the side with fewer gas molecules
the amount of product a reaction actually produces

look.title: Le Châtelier's Rule
look.text: Le Châtelier wrote that every system in stable chemical equilibrium, when subjected to an outside influence that tends to change its temperature or its condensation, whether as a whole or in one of its parts, can undergo only those internal changes which, if they occurred alone, would bring about a change of temperature or condensation in the opposite direction.
look.cite: Henry Le Châtelier, note to the French Academy of Sciences, 1884
look.prompt: Restate this rule in your own words in one sentence, then apply it to what happens when hydrogen is added to an ammonia equilibrium.

check.q: More hydrogen is added to a mixture of N2, H2 and NH3 at equilibrium. What happens?
choices: Nothing, because the equilibrium constant is fixed
The equilibrium shifts toward ammonia, using up some of the added hydrogen
The equilibrium shifts toward nitrogen and hydrogen
check.why: Adding a reactant disturbs the balance, and the system responds by consuming some of it to make more product.

check.q: Why does high pressure increase the yield of ammonia?
choices: The product side has fewer gas molecules, so it relieves the pressure
check.why: Four gas molecules become two. Shifting toward ammonia reduces the number of molecules and the pressure.

check.q: An exothermic reaction is at equilibrium. The mixture is heated. Which way does it shift, and why?
choices: Toward products, because heat speeds reactions
It cannot shift, because heat is not a chemical
Toward reactants, because heat acts like a product being added
check.why: For an exothermic reaction heat is on the product side, so adding heat pushes the balance back toward reactants.

lessons.title: Haber's Bargain
lessons.mainIdea: The Haber process balances yield against speed with moderate temperature, high pressure, an iron catalyst and removal of ammonia as it forms.
reading: The ammonia reaction, N2 + 3 H2 ⇌ 2 NH3, is exothermic and shrinks four gas molecules to two. Le Châtelier's principle says the best yield comes at low temperature and high pressure. But at low temperature the nitrogen triple bond almost never breaks; the reaction is far too slow to be useful. At high temperature the reaction is fast but the equilibrium lies toward the reactants. Neither extreme works. Haber's insight was that the answer had to be a *compromise*.

Modern plants run at roughly 400 to 500 °C and at pressures of about 150 to 250 atmospheres. The temperature is high enough for a reasonable rate and low enough for a usable yield. An *iron catalyst* lowers the activation energy so the rate at that temperature is acceptable. The catalyst does not change the equilibrium position, only how quickly it is reached. Even so, only a fraction of the gas turns to ammonia on each pass.

The rest of the trick is engineering. The mixture leaving the reactor is cooled until ammonia liquefies and is drained off, which removes product and, by Le Châtelier's principle, keeps pulling the reaction forward. The unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are pumped back through in a loop. Nothing is wasted. The cost is energy. Making the hydrogen from natural gas and compressing the gases takes a large amount of fuel, and the process is estimated to use about 1 to 2 percent of the world's energy supply. Feeding the world has never been free.

words.d: a middle choice between two goals that pull in opposite directions, such as speed and yield
the porous iron-based solid used in the Haber process to speed the reaction between nitrogen and hydrogen
the industrial method of making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen at high pressure with an iron catalyst
returning unreacted gases to the reactor so they get another chance to react

look.title: Two Dials and a Drain
look.text: Imagine a control room with a temperature dial, a pressure dial and a drain valve. Turn temperature up and the ammonia meter climbs quickly at first, then settles at a low level. Turn it down and the meter creeps up slowly toward a higher level, but so slowly the shift takes days. Turn pressure up and the level rises. Open the drain to draw off ammonia and the meter dips, then climbs back as fresh ammonia forms.
look.prompt: For each control, say whether it changes the rate, the equilibrium position, or both, and explain how the operator should set all three.

check.q: Why does the Haber process not run at a low temperature, even though that would give a higher yield?
choices: The catalyst melts at low temperature
The reaction would be far too slow
check.why: Yield and rate pull in opposite directions. A moderate temperature is a compromise between them.

check.q: What does the iron catalyst change in the Haber process?
choices: How fast equilibrium is reached, but not where it lies
The amount of ammonia at equilibrium
check.why: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both directions equally, so it speeds the approach to the same equilibrium.

check.q: Why is ammonia liquefied and removed as it forms?
choices: Removing product keeps the equilibrium shifting toward more ammonia
To increase the pressure in the reactor
check.why: By Le Châtelier's principle, taking away a product drives the reaction to replace it.

lessons.title: Redox in a Wire: Batteries
lessons.mainIdea: A battery separates the two halves of a redox reaction and forces the electrons to travel through a wire, where they can do work.
reading: In 1800 Alessandro Volta stacked disks of zinc and silver separated by cloth soaked in salt water and produced the first steady electric current. He had built a redox reaction into a machine. In any *electrochemical cell*, oxidation happens at one electrode, the *anode*, and reduction happens at the other, the *cathode*. Electrons released at the anode cannot cross the cell directly. They must go around through a wire, and on the way they can light a bulb or run a phone.

Different metals give up electrons with different eagerness. Zinc loses electrons far more readily than copper, so in a zinc-copper cell zinc is the anode. Chemists rank this eagerness on a table of standard reduction potentials, measured in volts against hydrogen. The farther apart two half-reactions sit on the table, the higher the *voltage* of a cell built from them. A salt bridge or porous barrier lets ions flow between the two halves to keep charges balanced, or the current would stop within moments.

Every battery you own is a variation on Volta's stack. An alkaline cell uses zinc and manganese dioxide and delivers about 1.5 volts. A car's lead-acid battery uses lead and lead dioxide, about 2 volts per cell, six cells in series. A lithium-ion cell moves lithium ions between a graphite anode and a metal oxide cathode at about 3.7 volts, and because lithium is so light it packs great energy per kilogram. Its inventors shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. A *rechargeable* battery is one whose redox reaction can be driven backward by pushing current in.

words.d: a device that produces electric current from a redox reaction, or uses current to drive one
the electrode where oxidation happens and electrons leave the cell
the electrode where reduction happens and electrons enter the cell
the electrical push of a cell, measured in volts; it depends on how different the two half-reactions are
describes a battery whose redox reaction can be reversed by applying an outside current

look.title: Standard Reduction Potentials
look.prompt: A more negative value means a metal gives up electrons more easily. Which metal here would be the anode in a cell with copper, and which pairing would give the highest voltage?

check.q: In an electrochemical cell, where does oxidation take place?
check.why: Oxidation, the loss of electrons, happens at the anode; the electrons then travel out through the wire.

check.q: Why do the electrons in a battery have to go through the wire?
choices: The two halves of the reaction are separated, so the wire is the only path
The salt bridge pushes them out
check.why: Separating oxidation from reduction forces the electron transfer to happen through the outside circuit, where it can do work.

check.q: Using the idea of reduction potentials, which pair of metals would make a cell with the highest voltage?
check.why: Voltage grows with the gap between the two potentials. Lithium and silver sit farthest apart.

lessons.title: Rust and How to Stop It
lessons.mainIdea: Corrosion is an unwanted electrochemical cell on a metal's surface, and it can be slowed by coatings, alloys or a more reactive sacrificial metal.
reading: *Corrosion* is redox you did not ask for. On a wet steel surface, one patch of iron becomes an anode and loses electrons, which travel through the metal to a nearby patch where oxygen and water accept them. Iron ions meet hydroxide, and rust, hydrated iron oxide, flakes off, exposing fresh metal. Dry iron barely rusts, because water is needed to carry ions. Salt water is worse, because dissolved ions conduct better and complete the circuit faster. Chicago's road salt attacks cars and bridges for exactly this reason.

One defense is to keep water and oxygen away. Paint, oil and plastic coatings all work until they are scratched. A better defense uses chemistry. Coating steel with zinc, called *galvanizing*, protects even when the zinc is scratched, because zinc is more easily oxidized than iron. The zinc becomes the anode and corrodes instead, while the iron becomes a cathode and stays intact. Highway guardrails and steel fence posts are galvanized for this reason.

The same idea protects ships and pipelines. A block of a very reactive metal such as magnesium or zinc is bolted to the steel hull or buried next to the pipe. It corrodes on purpose and is replaced every few years, while the steel it is wired to is spared. This is a *sacrificial anode*. Stainless steel takes another route: its chromium forms a thin, tough oxide film that seals the surface. Aluminum protects itself the same way, which is why aluminum cans and window frames do not crumble even though aluminum is more reactive than iron.

words.d: the slow destruction of a metal by redox reactions with its surroundings; rusting is corrosion of iron
coating steel with a layer of zinc, which corrodes in place of the iron
a block of a more reactive metal attached to a structure so that it corrodes instead of the structure
a thin, tightly bonded layer of metal oxide that seals a surface and stops further corrosion

look.title: Three Nails in Three Jars
look.text: Three identical iron nails sit in three jars for a week. The first jar holds dry air with a packet that absorbs moisture. The second holds tap water. The third holds salt water. At the end of the week the first nail is bright, the second has some orange rust, and the third is heavily rusted with a cloudy brown liquid around it.
look.prompt: Explain each result in terms of what corrosion needs. Then predict what would happen if a strip of zinc were wired to the nail in the salt-water jar.

check.q: Why does salt water speed up the rusting of iron?
choices: Salt reacts directly with iron to form rust
Dissolved ions carry charge better, completing the electrochemical circuit faster
Salt removes the oxygen from the water
check.why: Corrosion is an electrochemical cell, and a better conducting solution lets it run faster.

check.q: A galvanized steel post is scratched down to the iron. Why does the iron still not rust?
choices: The scratch seals itself with paint
Iron cannot rust once it has been galvanized
Zinc is more easily oxidized, so it corrodes first and protects the iron
The zinc forms a glass coating
check.why: Zinc acts as the anode, giving up its electrons in place of the iron.

check.q: Aluminum is more reactive than iron, yet an aluminum can does not crumble away. Why?
choices: Aluminum forms a thin, tough oxide film that seals its surface
check.why: The first layer of oxidation protects everything underneath, unlike flaky iron rust.

lessons.title: Forcing a Reaction Backward
lessons.mainIdea: Electrolysis uses an outside current to drive a redox reaction that would not happen on its own, which is how we make aluminum and split water.
reading: A battery lets a favorable redox reaction make electricity. *Electrolysis* runs the idea in reverse. Push current from an outside source through a liquid containing ions. You can then force electrons onto a substance that does not want them, and pull electrons off one that does not want to give them. Pass current through water with a little dissolved salt. Hydrogen bubbles rise at the cathode and oxygen bubbles rise at the anode. There is twice as much hydrogen as oxygen by volume, exactly as the formula H2O predicts.

Michael Faraday worked out the rules in 1834. The amount of substance produced at an electrode is proportional to the amount of electric charge passed. That link between charge and moles was an early clue that electricity comes in particles, and that atoms carry fixed amounts of it. Today it lets engineers calculate exactly how much metal a given current will deposit. That calculation is the basis of *electroplating*, the coating of a cheap metal with a thin layer of chromium, silver or gold.

Electrolysis built the modern world's lightest structural metal. Aluminum is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust. But it clings to oxygen so tightly that no ordinary chemical reaction frees it, and in the 1850s it cost more than silver. In 1886 Charles Hall in Ohio and Paul Héroult in France independently found the answer. Aluminum oxide dissolved in *molten* cryolite could be electrolyzed to give pure metal. The *Hall-Héroult process* still makes all the world's aluminum. Its enormous hunger for electricity is why recycling a can saves roughly 95 percent of the energy of making a new one.

words.d: using an electric current to drive a redox reaction that would not happen on its own
using electrolysis to coat an object with a thin layer of metal
the industrial method of making aluminum by electrolyzing aluminum oxide dissolved in molten cryolite
melted into a liquid, as ionic compounds must be for their ions to move and carry current

look.title: Faraday Links Charge to Chemistry
look.text: Faraday reported that the chemical power of a current of electricity is in direct proportion to the absolute quantity of electricity which passes. He found that the same quantity of electricity decomposes chemically equivalent amounts of different substances, whatever the substance, and suggested that the atoms of matter are in some way endowed with electrical powers.
look.cite: Michael Faraday, Experimental Researches in Electricity, seventh series, 1834
look.prompt: Faraday found that a fixed amount of charge always frees a fixed amount of a substance. What does that suggest about how electric charge and atoms are related?

check.q: What is the key difference between a battery and electrolysis?
choices: A battery uses a favorable redox reaction to make current; electrolysis uses current to force a non-favorable one
Electrolysis uses metals and batteries do not
check.why: Electrolysis is a battery run backward, with the outside current supplying the energy.

check.q: When water is electrolyzed, why is twice as much hydrogen gas produced as oxygen gas?
choices: Hydrogen is lighter and rises faster
Each water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom
Oxygen dissolves back into the water
Hydrogen is produced at both electrodes
check.why: Atoms are conserved, so the ratio of gases matches the formula H2O.

check.q: Why was aluminum more expensive than silver before 1886?
choices: Aluminum is rare in Earth's crust
Aluminum ore was found only in France
Aluminum bonds so strongly to oxygen that no ordinary chemical reaction could free it
check.why: Only electrolysis, discovered by Hall and Héroult, could supply the energy to pull aluminum away from oxygen cheaply.

review.q: Which statement is a direct consequence of the law of conservation of mass?
choices: Every chemical equation must be balanced
review.why: Since atoms are neither created nor destroyed, the same atoms must appear on both sides.

review.q: In the reaction Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu, which substance is reduced?
review.why: The copper ion gains two electrons to become copper metal, which is reduction.

review.q: Which change would NOT increase the rate of a reaction between a solid and a solution?
review.why: Dilution lowers concentration, so collisions happen less often and the rate falls.

review.q: What does a catalyst change, and what does it leave unchanged?
choices: It changes the products but not the rate
It changes ΔH but not the activation energy
It changes the equilibrium constant but not the rate
It lowers the activation energy but leaves the equilibrium position the same
review.why: A catalyst speeds both directions equally by offering a lower path; the final balance is unchanged.

review.q: A reaction at equilibrium has forward and reverse rates that are
choices: unequal, with the forward rate larger
review.why: Dynamic equilibrium means both reactions continue at the same rate.

review.q: For the exothermic reaction N2 + 3 H2 ⇌ 2 NH3, which combination gives the highest yield of ammonia at equilibrium?
review.why: Cooling favors the exothermic direction, and pressure favors the side with fewer gas molecules. Rate is a separate problem.

review.q: Why does a zinc coating protect steel even after it is scratched?
choices: Zinc is oxidized more easily than iron, so it corrodes in place of the steel
Zinc turns iron into stainless steel
review.why: Zinc acts as a sacrificial anode, giving up electrons so the iron does not.

review.q: Which process requires an outside source of electric current?
choices: A lithium-ion battery powering a phone
Iron rusting on a wet bridge
A zinc-copper cell lighting a bulb
review.why: Aluminum production is electrolysis, a reaction forced to run against its natural direction by an outside current.
